Here's the bad news: For anything other than a shotgun you won't find much powder or bullets, and primers are nationally gone!

If you are going to reload for a shotgun you are in good shape. (However, plenty of shotgun ammo on the shelves so buy that 1st.)

A Lee Load-All is ~$75 @ Bass Pro Shop & elsewhere. (I got one when I was 16 and reloaded shells correctly 1st try, it's easy.)

https://www.titanreloading.com/image/cache/data/D2g/LoadAll2_3-600x600.jpg

Buy a shotshell reloading manual and determine what you want to load for (bird, slug, buckshot) that all share the same powder.

https://media.mwstatic.com/product-images/880x660/Primary/887/887011.jpg

Red Dot, Green Dot, Longshot, etc. can be used across many load types. (some work for handguns too)

Track down that powder and figure 1 lb. = 300-400 reloads from it. (depends on your charge per shell)

Go buy a pile of 209 primers, they are cheap and there are plenty out there.

Figure out what wads you need (reloading manual) and buy them, $10-12 / 250.

Go buy used hulls, they sell for ~$10-12 / 100.

Go buy shot / buck / slugs to fill those hulls with.

Consider buying molds (Lee, etc.) so you can make your own slugs & buck from scrap lead (car battery).

Spend a weekend cranking out shells.
So you decided to get into reloading...

I'll add, as a long time gun owner the shotgun remains the most versatile firearm there is -

Change the load for game (deer, waterfowl, upland birds) or for self-defense.

Change the barrel for close range (18-21" cylinder choke) or distance (rifled / slug or full choke)

Add a magazine extension to increase capacity by 2-3 rounds

A pump shotgun is nearly impervious to shell loading errors like undercharging (won't cycle semi-auto action)

A 12 gauge is probably the best "does it all" gauge

I have been reloading for years, I used to own v/bulletbuilder. I have never loaded shot shells despite having a multistage loader. That's about to change because I just acquired a 16gauge bolt-action.

Is there any benefit to ordering brass hulls?

Yes, if you can get them but they are in short supply because of SASS (cowboy action shooting) and they are ex$pen$ive. The main benefit is that if cared for (annealed periodically) they could last for 50+ reloads or more. So for the longterm/prepper scenario with little chance of resupply they make sense.

I don't own any however, price has always held me back and used hulls (right now) are plentiful & cheap. I have not looked it up but believe you can get 6+ reloads from plastic hulls before the crimp becomes unusable. When that happens you can switch to a roll crimp & shot cards and probably get another 6+ from them (this is a guess). With your 16 gauge however (superb gauge), plastic hulls will likely always be cheap because so few own anything that shoots it.

Roll crimps w/ cards vs star crimp -

Roll crimp tool (goes in hand drill or drill press) -

The crimping is why I never got into reloading shot shells. The brass shells came to mind because I was thinking about a last resort gun. I think you could sill the shells with wax and charge with black powder.

Yes, with brass shells you basically just put a wad over the shot column, seal it, and call it a day. The old timey way is with something called "water glass". If is a clear liquid that solidifies like glue. You can also use white Elmer's. And yes, BP is definitely an option and how it is done in SASS.

If you are using previously fired hulls to reload with, the crimp is already there. The Load-All just resets the crimp to the original position. Below is a pic showing a Load-all "re-crimp". You can see some of them go inward (bottom row) because the reloader did not have his shot column height correct. That could be from the wad, not enough shot, etc. There are many techniques to deal with that (filler cards, longer/shorter wads, etc.). The top row is correct though, all the internally parts are sized properly.

https://i217.photobucket.com/albums/cc190/aristico/20160327_152719_zpsyvqw6oga.jpg

Longer durability I'd imagine. Plastic shells can be reloaded numerous times before they start to crack though. Do your research though because the majority of plastic shells are not said to be safe to reload. Winchester AA shells and Remington something is what most people use.

I can't find any specific source as to what ones are safe/unsafe, but when I was first starting out, I was warned against cheap disposable shells, especially those with cardboard base on the interior.

The logic behind it is that there's a risk of the cardboard/plastic loosening up and getting lodged inside your barrel, as well as no load data for it.

Protip: many commercial hulls can be reused, but not all. Rio Royal Buck brand shotgun shells are low quality, harder plastic, and do not uncrimp into a regular 2 3/4 inch shell after firing.

They have a strange disc that flies out the front instead.

You can recrimp those with a roll crimper not a star crimper. To get even further into the weeds, roll crimp hull as unskived. Hulls meant to be star crimped are skived. Basically the open end is thinned in a skived shell to allow it to be folded over with the star crimper. Unskived ones are left thick so when the roll crimper heats & rolls them they stay rolled up.

The disc is a a clear shot card -
